paragraphs: This paper compares a model of cortical map formation with optical images of monkey visual cortex. The images capture several properties together: preferred line orientation, how selectively a location responds to orientation, and its preference for input from either eye. Seeing these properties across large cortical areas makes it possible to examine both nearby relationships and broader spatial organization.

The model treats this organization as a mapping from five feature dimensions onto the two-dimensional cortical surface. Two dimensions describe retinal position, while the others describe orientation preference, orientation specificity, and ocular dominance. The central organizing requirement is that the mapping preserve neighborhood relationships locally, even while fitting these different features onto one surface.

The quantitative analysis finds that this mapping principle produces correlations between orientation selectivity and ocular dominance seen in the imaging data. The result supports topology preservation as a candidate organizing principle for visual cortex. Its significance is the connection between a general mathematical constraint and specific relationships among experimentally observed cortical maps.
neurips-1991-a-comparison-between-a-neur.tldr: A topology-preserving map model explains observed relationships among orientation tuning and eye preference in monkey visual cortex.

paragraphs: The paper compares two ways to train feedforward networks for regression, where the goal is to predict numerical outputs without starting from a prescribed model of the underlying relationship. Both approaches build predictions using projections of the inputs, but they differ in how they learn the nonlinear transformations applied within the network.

Backpropagation learning uses a fully parametric formulation. Projection pursuit learning instead estimates unknown nonlinear functions nonparametrically, proceeding through neurons and layers in sequence at each iteration while also estimating connection weights. This gives the second approach flexibility in the shapes of its learned functions, rather than restricting learning to the parameters of a completely specified functional form.

With Gauss–Newton optimization, the two methods have comparable training speeds, while projection pursuit produces a more economical model. The comparison also finds backpropagation more sensitive to noise outliers. Together, these findings separate three considerations that can otherwise be conflated: computational speed, model economy, and robustness to unusual observations. Similar training speed does not imply similar behavior on the other two.
neurips-1991-a-comparison-of-projection-.tldr: Projection pursuit matches backpropagation’s training speed under Gauss–Newton optimization while producing more economical models and showing less sensitivity to outliers.

paragraphs: This paper uses neural learning experiments to study linguistic stress: the patterns determining which syllables receive emphasis. Its question concerns not only how to describe these patterns, but also how easy they are to learn. The authors position measured learning behavior as an empirical alternative to arguments based on logically deducing linguistic parameter settings from an initial state.

The experiments train perceptrons on data from nineteen human languages. From these experiments, the authors develop a characterization using six parameters. These parameters serve two purposes: they partially describe a language’s stress pattern and predict its learnability. The characterization does not require theoretical structures such as metrical feet, which appear in traditional analyses.

The contribution is therefore a link between descriptive linguistic categories and the behavior of a learning system. A useful description should capture aspects of the patterns while also helping explain differences in learning difficulty. The work demonstrates how machine learning experiments can inform linguistic analysis, with the learnability conclusions grounded in the perceptron experiments described.
neurips-1991-a-connectionist-learning-ap.tldr: Perceptron experiments on nineteen languages yield six parameters that describe stress patterns and predict their learnability.

paragraphs: The paper models how the brainstem and cerebellum cooperate to make accurate saccades, the rapid eye movements that shift gaze. It uses feedback-error learning: a feedback controller supplies an error signal that teaches another component how to improve movement control. Here, the superior colliculus serves as a simple controller without knowledge of the eye’s initial position.

The cerebellum is represented by a CMAC learning model. It learns to compensate for nonlinear eye-muscle behavior by adjusting the gain of an internal feedback loop in the brainstem’s burst generator. This changes the size of the burst delivered to motoneurons, linking the learned correction to the command that moves the eye.

Using errors that indicate direction alone, the system rapidly learns accurate horizontal movements from any starting position. It also adapts realistically when the simulations weaken eye muscles or shift the target. These findings show how a relatively limited teaching signal can support adaptive accuracy through an interaction between feedback circuitry and a learned adjustment mechanism.
neurips-1991-a-neural-net-model-for-adap.tldr: A brainstem–cerebellum model learns accurate horizontal eye movements from direction-only errors and adapts to simulated muscle and target changes.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural network that finds pattern boundaries and identifies the patterns at the same time. Segmentation asks where one object ends and another begins; recognition asks what each object is. The proposed architecture combines these tasks and self-organizes to detect both the locations of input patterns and their boundaries.

The authors demonstrate the approach on character recognition using the NIST database. The examples include situations in which visual separation is difficult: characters touch or overlap, characters are broken, and images contain noise. In such inputs, deciding which image parts belong together is closely connected to deciding which character those parts form.

The reported result is high accuracy while performing segmentation and recognition simultaneously across these difficult cases. This matters because the system addresses ambiguity in boundaries as part of the recognition task itself. Its contribution is an integrated architecture that handles both character identity and spatial organization, showing that imperfect separation does not have to be resolved before recognition can proceed.
neurips-1991-a-self-organizing-integrate.tldr: A self-organizing network jointly locates and recognizes characters, including touching, overlapping, broken, and noisy examples.

paragraphs: This paper explains how Bayesian model comparison can guide decisions about feedforward neural networks. It distinguishes fitting parameters within a chosen model from comparing different models. That distinction matters because finding suitable weights for a network does not, by itself, determine whether its architecture or regularization choices are appropriate.

The framework incorporates a Bayesian version of Occam’s razor and supports comparisons between solutions using different network architectures. It also provides a basis for choosing both the strength and the form of weight decay, which discourages particular weight configurations during fitting. These choices become parts of a common inference framework rather than unrelated adjustments.

The framework additionally produces uncertainty estimates for network parameters and outputs, along with an effective parameter count reflecting how many parameters the data actually determine. This distinguishes the network’s nominal size from its data-supported complexity. The paper also discusses connections to predicting generalization, bringing model selection, regularization, uncertainty, and effective complexity into one account of neural-network modeling.
neurips-1991-bayesian-model-comparison-a.tldr: Bayesian model comparison provides a unified approach to network architecture selection, weight decay, uncertainty estimation, and effective model complexity.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a simple neural network can produce synchronized bursts of activity. Its neurons are binary, every neuron excites every other neuron, and inhibition acts globally across the network. The authors analyze this architecture mathematically and numerically, connecting its wiring and input conditions to the activity it generates.

For random input signals, they prove that the network produces synchronized bursts separated by apparently random stretches of noisy activity. Their interpretation is that the architecture amplifies incoming signals that happen to coincide. Coordinated output can therefore arise through amplification of coincident inputs, without requiring the network to settle into a shared repeating frequency.

Damped oscillations accompany this synchronization, but the analysis finds that they do not contribute constructively to it. They are a side effect of the dynamics rather than the mechanism responsible for the bursts. This distinction matters when interpreting neural activity: observing oscillations alongside synchrony does not establish that the oscillations generate that synchrony, as this solvable model illustrates.
neurips-1991-burst-synchronization-witho.tldr: A simple excitatory network with global inhibition produces synchronized bursts by amplifying coincident inputs, while accompanying oscillations are incidental.

paragraphs: This paper uses constrained optimization to tune the operating parameters of analog circuits automatically. The authors apply the method to a three-transistor square-root circuit and an analog VLSI artificial cochlea. The task is to make the behavior of a physical chip match a specified goal as closely as possible.

Computer-controlled measurement and test equipment measures the circuit’s behavior while the optimization method chooses its parameters. The objective is to reduce the difference between actual and desired behavior. This addresses two practical needs identified in the paper: compensating for manufacturing deviations and adjusting performance within the circuit’s available operating range.

The broader motivation is that increasingly complex biologically inspired circuits expose more parameters, making manual adjustment cumbersome. The work treats tuning as an integral part of engineering design: construct a circuit with enough adjustable behavior, then automatically select settings for a particular goal. Its significance lies in connecting physical measurements to parameter selection, so that desired behavior guides the tuning of the actual device.
neurips-1991-constrained-optimization-ap.tldr: Constrained optimization and computer-controlled measurements automatically tune analog circuits toward specified behavior.

paragraphs: This paper outlines an adaptive control scheme for tasks in which a controller repeatedly receives its current state and chooses an action toward a state-dependent goal. Its central priority is learning adequate behavior with few experimental control decisions while remaining robust. The authors argue that extra computation and memory can be acceptable costs for achieving those priorities.

The scheme is framed around learning forward models and introduces memory-based learning as a way to use past experience. Input–output pairs are explicitly stored. When a new prediction is needed, the system retrieves experiences with nearby inputs and uses them to estimate a locally consistent output. The supplied text discusses nearest-neighbor, kernel-regression, and locally weighted regression techniques.

The important tradeoff is between the expense of computation during a control cycle and the expense of learning through actions. The paper motivates spending available processing capacity to reduce undesirable learning behavior, including excessive trial decisions or becoming stuck. It presents this as a design direction for effective control, rather than reporting a measured performance improvement in the supplied passage.
neurips-1991-fast-robust-adaptive-contro.tldr: The paper proposes prioritizing robust, experience-efficient adaptive control by spending more computation and memory on learned forward models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a health-monitoring approach for the pointing system of a large antenna used in deep-space communications. The task is to diagnose system faults from monitored signals. The authors combine neural networks with signal-processing methods, presenting the application as a hybrid monitoring problem rather than treating neural classification as the entire solution.

The proposed approach includes autoregressive modeling, pattern recognition, and Hidden Markov models. These components bring signal modeling and recognition into the same monitoring system. A central issue is detecting classes that were absent from the training data. For fault diagnosis, this matters because a monitor may encounter behavior that does not belong to any previously learned fault category.

The authors report experimental results indicating reliability sufficient for practical implementation. That finding supports the combined approach in the antenna-monitoring setting studied. The broader methodological contribution is its attention to problems shared by other monitoring applications, especially how to recognize that an observation represents an unfamiliar class instead of assuming training has covered every possibility.
neurips-1991-fault-diagnosis-of-antenna-.tldr: A hybrid neural and signal-processing system diagnoses antenna-pointing faults while addressing fault classes missing from training.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to train recurrent neural networks online, as their activity unfolds. It identifies a tradeoff in existing methods: backward propagation through time requires a backward pass for accumulating errors, while forward learning can operate online but incurs substantial computation when updating a large sensitivity matrix.

The proposed method replaces direct integration of the high-dimensional sensitivity dynamics with a forward calculation of their Green’s function. This reformulation avoids redundant computations, after which weights can be updated when an error needs correction. The authors describe the resulting algorithm as one order faster per time step than the sensitivity-matrix approach.

A numerical example classifies state trajectories with a recurrent network and supports the claimed speed advantage over the Williams–Zipser algorithm. The significance is that online operation and computational efficiency are addressed together. The method retains a forward-in-time learning procedure while changing the calculation needed to connect network errors to weight updates, targeting a specific computational bottleneck in recurrent learning.
neurips-1991-green-s-function-method-for.tldr: A Green’s-function formulation reduces redundant sensitivity calculations to accelerate online recurrent-network learning.

paragraphs: HARMONET is a system that expands a single melody into a four-part chorale in the style of J. S. Bach. The authors train its neural networks using error backpropagation on roughly a dozen Bach chorales. The task is musical production: the system must generate a harmonized piece from the supplied melodic line.

The authors attribute its capabilities to two design choices. First, a new representation captures musically relevant information. Second, a hierarchical architecture combines backpropagation-trained networks with symbolic algorithms. The representation determines what musical information is available to the learning system, while the hierarchy brings learned processing and explicit symbolic procedures into one solution.

The paper reports performance suitable for musical practice. This is a claim about completing the harmonization task in a useful musical form, rather than merely recognizing patterns in existing compositions. The broader contribution is an example of how a neural system’s practical abilities can depend on its input coding and its integration with other algorithms, alongside learning from examples.
neurips-1991-harmonet-a-neural-net-for-h.tldr: HARMONET combines neural learning, musical representations, and symbolic algorithms to turn a melody into a Bach-style four-part chorale.

paragraphs: This paper studies incremental learning when the rule being learned changes over time. A learner continually updates its hypothesis while an adversary modifies the target concept. The objective is to keep the learner’s predictions close to the current target, making ongoing tracking accuracy the central issue rather than eventual convergence to one fixed rule.

The framework is distribution-free and examines two geometric concept classes: a single half-plane and the intersection of two half-planes. A half-plane describes the region on one side of a straight boundary. The analysis connects the learner’s average mistake rate to the maximum rate at which the adversary can change the target concept.

Simulations of several learning algorithms, including backpropagation, verify the theoretical predictions. The important implication is that learning performance depends on how quickly the target is allowed to move. The work provides a way to reason about this dependence explicitly, tying the difficulty of tracking a changing rule to a constraint on the source of that change.
neurips-1991-incrementally-learning-time.tldr: A theory of incremental learning links mistakes on changing half-plane concepts to the maximum speed of adversarial change.

paragraphs: This paper trains second-order recurrent networks to recognize simple finite-state languages made from binary strings. Training uses both positive examples, which belong to the language, and negative examples, which do not. The task is to infer a sequential acceptance rule from examples and then apply it to strings beyond those used during learning.

The authors use the complete gradient of the recurrent network during optimization. They report solutions that recognize strings of arbitrary length when the training examples sufficiently constrain the language being induced. That condition is important: successful recognition depends on the examples providing enough information to distinguish the intended language from alternatives consistent with limited observations.

The paper also demonstrates a method for extracting a finite-state automaton corresponding to an optimized network. This connects the learned recurrent computation to an explicit state-based representation of the language. Together, the results address both generalization across string lengths and the possibility of turning a trained neural recognizer into a symbolic account of its sequential behavior.
neurips-1991-induction-of-finite-state-a.tldr: Second-order recurrent networks learn simple binary finite-state languages, and corresponding automata can be extracted from the trained networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies a generative form of generalization: producing letter shapes in a new font after seeing only a few examples from it. The authors design and train a connectionist network for this task. To succeed, the system must represent both which letter is being produced and the visual style shared by letters in the font.

During training, the network develops distributed internal representations of letters and fonts. Each training example contains both kinds of information simultaneously, so the learned representations distinguish factors that arrive together in the observed letterform. This separation gives the system a way to relate a small set of font examples to the production of further letterforms.

The architecture is central to the reported result. Separate but interconnected hidden units for letter and font representations were necessary in the authors’ experiments, while several alternatives were unsuccessful. The finding connects productive generalization to how internal representations are organized: the two factors need distinct representations, along with connections that allow them to jointly determine the output.
neurips-1991-network-generalization-for-.tldr: A network generates letters in a new font from a few examples by learning separate, interconnected representations of letter identity and font.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural network model whose temporal sequencing depends on its modulatory state. Temporal sequencing concerns how activity develops in an ordered progression over time. The model is motivated by neurocognitive observations of waking and sleeping, making changes in overall brain state central to the behavior the authors seek to explain.

Computer studies examine the network under different aminergic and cholinergic modulatory influences. They demonstrate that distinct sequencing states can occur within the same network. The key result is therefore a change in the organization of activity associated with modulation, rather than a requirement to introduce a different network for each sequencing state.

The paper discusses how this state dependence relates to memory, sequencing, and learning. Its explanatory value is that a shared network can support different temporal behaviors under different influences. This makes modulatory state part of the account of what the network does: understanding its sequence behavior requires considering both the network itself and the conditions under which its activity unfolds.
neurips-1991-network-model-of-state-depe.tldr: A neural network exhibits distinct temporal sequencing states under different aminergic and cholinergic modulation.

paragraphs: This paper develops networks for recovering source signals from mixtures involving time delays or filtering. In these settings, the observed mixture reflects more than the simultaneous addition of source values: timing and signal transformations also affect what reaches the separator. The aim is to recover the component signals despite those effects.

The authors first show that a subset of the Herault–Jutten learning rules satisfies a minimum-output-power principle. They then use that principle to guide extensions of the Herault–Jutten network with delays in the feedback path. The theoretical connection gives the extended architecture a common objective linking its learning behavior to the original rules.

The resulting networks perform well on real speech and music signals mixed using delays or filtering. These examples support the approach for signals with the temporal structure relevant to the stated separation problem. The contribution combines an interpretation of existing learning rules with an architectural extension, showing how a shared optimization principle can guide networks toward handling more complicated mixtures.
neurips-1991-networks-for-the-separation.tldr: Networks with delayed feedback use a minimum-output-power principle to separate speech and music mixtures involving delays or filtering.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether brain recordings can help automatically monitor vigilance during attention-intensive work. The authors train feedforward neural networks with backpropagation to interpret event-related potentials and electroencephalogram signals associated with high and low vigilance. The intended application is a monitoring instrument that also tracks the attentiveness of its operator.

On an event-related-potential dataset averaged over 28 minutes, the network achieves 96% accuracy, compared with 83% for linear discriminant analysis. This result indicates that the neural approach captures information useful for distinguishing vigilance states in those averaged recordings. However, such a long observation window does not meet the paper’s stated need for practical monitoring over shorter periods.

The authors therefore also examine shorter recordings. Averaging event-related potentials over two minutes still yields 90% correct prediction of a vigilance measure. EEG power-spectrum segments lasting only 56 seconds provide similarly good performance. These results make the time window a central part of the finding: useful vigilance prediction remains possible with substantially shorter observations in the reported analysis.
neurips-1991-neural-network-analysis-of-.tldr: Neural networks predict vigilance from brain recordings, retaining 90% accuracy with two-minute event-related-potential averages.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural network for planning mobile-robot paths through a two-dimensional workspace. A valid path must connect the initial and final positions while remaining in the region the robot can occupy. The goal is to find a valid path that also satisfies an optimality criterion, so avoiding obstacles is only part of the planning problem.

The network is arranged as a two-dimensional sheet of neurons that collectively represents the workspace. Cooperative lateral connections cause the sheet to oscillate. The authors use those oscillations to generate solutions of Bellman’s dynamic programming equation for path planning, linking the network’s evolving activity to a mathematical formulation of optimal routes.

Simulation experiments suggest that the networks find globally optimal paths even with substantial circuit noise. The stated evidence therefore supports both the planning mechanism and its tolerance of noisy circuit behavior in simulation. The distinctive contribution is the use of oscillatory distributed computation to solve the planning equation, giving the network’s dynamics a direct role in determining a route.
neurips-1991-oscillatory-neural-fields-f.tldr: An oscillating neural sheet solves a dynamic-programming path-planning equation and finds globally optimal routes in noisy simulations.

paragraphs: This paper models how connections from retinal ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate nucleus become organized during visual development in cats. The developing projections acquire both eye-specific layering and a precise spatial map. Because normal development depends on retinal activity, the authors investigate how patterns of activity could help shape this organization.

The simulations combine three ingredients: waves of activity traveling across the retina, Hebbian competition among synapses, and earlier arrival of axons from the opposite eye. Retinal waves provide correlated activity across cells, while competitive synaptic change and arrival timing influence how projections develop. The proposed explanation therefore depends on these mechanisms acting together.

The authors report that the simulations account for observed projection patterns in both normal animals and animals subjected to experimental treatments. This links an observed form of early retinal activity to later anatomical organization through explicit developmental mechanisms. The result supports the sufficiency of the combined model for reproducing those patterns, connecting activity correlations, competition, and developmental timing in one explanation.
neurips-1991-retinogeniculate-developmen.tldr: Simulations combine retinal activity waves, synaptic competition, and axon arrival timing to explain developing eye-specific and spatial projection patterns.

paragraphs: This paper introduces RuleNet, a neural network that learns explicit condition–action rules in a formal string-manipulation domain. Alongside these symbolic rules, it learns functional categories of domain elements. The categories provide groupings over which rules can operate, connecting learned internal organization to an explicit description of what action should follow a condition.

Learning proceeds through a process called iterative projection. At selected points, the system extracts rules from its developing representations, inserts those rules back into the network, and continues training. Rule extraction therefore changes subsequent learning. The symbolic representation participates in the training process rather than serving only as a final explanation of a trained system.

The authors report improved learning and generalization compared with alternative neural-network approaches. They also argue that learned categories give the architecture capabilities beyond a purely symbolic system. An application to case-role assignment in natural language processing demonstrates a rule-based solution. The contribution is the recurring interaction between category discovery and explicit rules, with each contributing to the system’s continuing development.
neurips-1991-rule-induction-through-inte.tldr: RuleNet improves learning and generalization by repeatedly extracting symbolic rules and feeding them back into neural training.

paragraphs: This paper develops a segmentation algorithm based on an absolute-value smoothness penalty. Such a penalty controls how neighboring values are encouraged to agree during optimization. The authors use it in place of the more common quadratic regularizer, obtaining a formulation that imposes a piecewise-constant structure on the segmented data.

The optimization energy is convex, and the paper reports a unique global minimum. This means the solution procedure avoids the problem of getting trapped in inferior local minima. The authors also state that complicated continuation methods are unnecessary. The choice of smoothness penalty thus affects both the form of the segmentation and the difficulty of finding its optimum.

The work connects this mathematical formulation to a physical implementation by interpreting the energy as generalized power in a nonlinear resistive network. Using that interpretation, the authors construct a continuous-time analog segmentation circuit. The contribution spans the objective and its implementation: a particular segmentation constraint is expressed through a convex optimization problem that can also be realized as circuit dynamics.
neurips-1991-segmentation-circuits-using.tldr: An absolute-value smoothness penalty yields convex, piecewise-constant segmentation and supports a continuous-time analog circuit implementation.

paragraphs: This paper examines optimization-based explanations of arm movement, focusing on the minimum-muscle-tension-change model. The model identifies changes in muscle tension as the quantity to minimize when generating a movement. The study places that proposal alongside other optimization techniques used in arm-control models, asking what movement behavior follows from this particular choice of objective.

The authors use a dynamic simulator of a monkey’s arm containing seventeen muscles. These include muscles acting across one joint and muscles acting across two joints. The simulator generates horizontal hand movements, linking a muscle-level optimization criterion to the resulting motion of the hand through an explicit model of arm dynamics.

The paper discusses the hand trajectories produced by the algorithm. These trajectories are the observable consequences through which the proposed control objective is investigated. The study’s contribution is to make the movement criterion concrete in a multi-muscle simulation: minimizing changes in muscle tension must produce a path through the coordinated action of muscles and joints, rather than specifying the hand path directly.
neurips-1991-simulation-of-optimal-movem.tldr: A seventeen-muscle monkey-arm simulation explores the hand trajectories generated by minimizing changes in muscle tension.

paragraphs: This paper studies mathematical connections among spline approximation, rational-function approximation, and feedforward neural networks. All three provide ways to represent or approximate functions. By relating them, the authors investigate neural-network approximation through a broader mathematical setting, with attention to how closely the available representation can match a target function.

One question is whether moving from one hidden layer to two can improve the degree of approximation. The paper examines the potential gain from this architectural change. This frames depth as a question about representational accuracy: adding a layer matters insofar as it changes what approximation quality the network can achieve.

The authors also extend results concerning spline knot locations chosen according to the probability distribution of examples rather than the target’s function values. Knot locations determine where the spline’s pieces meet, so their placement is part of the approximation design. This distinction connects attainable accuracy to the information used in constructing the representation, separating where examples occur from what output values they carry.
neurips-1991-splines-rational-functions-.tldr: The paper connects neural-network approximation to splines and rational functions, examining hidden-layer depth and distribution-based knot placement.

paragraphs: This paper derives training criteria for turning adaptive classifiers into unsupervised data analyzers. The starting point is a classifier that outputs a probability vector over possible classes. Instead of relying on supplied classification labels, the proposed criteria guide how the network organizes its interpretations of the input data.

The first criterion converts a simple Gaussian classifier into a Gaussian-mixture analyzer. The second applies more broadly and uses mutual information. It reduces to a difference between two entropy terms: one encourages decisive interpretations, while the other encourages fairness among the available alternatives. The objective brings these two pressures together rather than rewarding confidence alone.

The general criterion can be applied to any network with probability-like outputs, creating a bridge from supervised classifier architectures to unsupervised analysis. However, the authors explicitly note that it does not necessarily produce useful behavior. Its broad applicability therefore concerns where the objective can be used; it does not guarantee that the resulting classifications will reveal a useful organization of the data.
neurips-1991-unsupervised-classifiers-mu.tldr: Mutual-information criteria turn probabilistic classifiers toward unsupervised learning by balancing decisive assignments with fair use of alternative classes.
